To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we can use Siamese networks to learn a reward function from a single demonstration that enables an agent to learn to perform a task by imitation, 2) the inclusion of an additional encoding loss helps to balance reward for the specific instance of a task versus the task in general, 3) the inclusion of multi-domain data helps the agent learn a more generalizable policy, and 4) we can apply this approach to 2D and 3D agents

(1) we propose a method that uses a Siamese network for computing a distance between a demonstrated motion and the current agent’s motion, (2) this distance is used as the RL reward, and (3) this method is shown to be effective on both 2D and 3D humanoid agents with 10 and 38 DoF respectively.

1) a Siamese network can be trained to provide a reward for visual imitation, and 2) the inclusion of multi-modal data, an image encoding loss, and a temporal loss helps the Siamese network provide a more useful reward signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of learning a policy from a single demonstration in a one-shot setting.
the question: Can a reinforcement learning agent learn to imitate a demonstration by only watching the demonstration?
how an RL agent can learn a task by watching a single demonstration of that task.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Siamese networks are able to learn the desired motion and reward from a demonstration and can be used as a comparator for a reinforcement learning based policy.

the inclusion of a Siamese network as a comparator in the RL framework is a promising way to learn behaviours from a single demonstration, and that multi-task learning and an image encoding loss are useful to balance reward for specific instances and general behaviours.
we have developed a novel Siamese network architecture that can compute a temporal distance between motion clips.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our approach can learn a variety of complex behaviours with only a single demonstration and can generalize well to unseen tasks.
we have demonstrated that it is possible to train a policy to imitate an expert’s behaviour using Siamese networks as a reward signal, without any additional information such as the reward function.
we have shown that Siamese networks provide a viable method for learning visual imitation from a single demonstration, and that this method scales well to 3D humanoid agents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Siamese networks provide a simple yet powerful mechanism to provide reward for imitation learning tasks.
a Siamese network can provide a useful reward for imitation learning.
Siamese Networks can be a viable solution for learning visual imitation in a one-shot learning setting.
